name: Base Rate Fallacy
description: People often underweight general statistical base-rate information when a vivid or representative case description is available, letting the specific story dominate the probabilities.
design_relevance_note: Relevant anywhere teams overreact to vivid anecdotes while ignoring population data: user-research synthesis, fraud/risk triage, personalization, content moderation, support prioritization, and experiment interpretation.
myth_risk_note: The popular claim that humans are broadly, inherently unable to use base-rate information is disputed by a substantial body of work (Koehler 1996; Cosmides & Tooby 1996; Christensen-Szalanski & Beach 1982; Gigerenzer 1991) showing the effect is highly dependent on information format (single-event probability vs. natural frequency) and task experience, and largely disappears under more ecologically realistic conditions.
prevalence_note: A canonical heuristics-and-biases example in decision-science teaching and one of the standard cautionary cases for probability reasoning in applied research and product work.

findings.description: Under representativeness judgments, people systematically neglect prior probabilities/base rates when a case description feels diagnostic or stereotype-consistent, allowing similarity-to-type to dominate statistical reasoning. This is the classic representativeness mechanism behind what later literature and practice call the base rate fallacy.
findings.source_title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases

applications.title: Bar-Hillel's 'cab problem': ignoring base rates in a hit-and-run scenario
applications.description: In a foundational study, Maya Bar-Hillel presented participants with a scenario involving two cab companies in a city (85% of cabs 'Blue,' 15% 'Green'). A witness to a hit-and-run identifies the cab as green and is shown to be 80% accurate at distinguishing the two colors. Most participants estimated an 80% probability that the cab was actually green, ignoring the base rate; the correct probability, accounting for how rare green cabs are, is 41%.
applications.industry_context: legal/judicial decision-making (illustrative study design), probability-judgment research
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, quantified finding from a foundational probability-judgment study, not a persuasion or product-design case -- included because Base Rate Fallacy, like several other classical logical-fallacy entries in this corpus, doesn't have a natural 'product' shape, and grounding it in a real, disclosed, peer-reviewed study is more honest than leaving it purely definitional.
